title: Data Loss Prevention Across M365 and Endpoints
monthTitle: Data Security & AI Governance with Microsoft Purview
summary: Classification tells you what your sensitive data is; Data Loss Prevention decides what people are allowed to do with it. This lesson builds Microsoft Purview DLP policies that span Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and managed devices through Endpoint DLP. You will learn to write conditions from Sensitive Information Types and sensitivity labels, choose actions from policy tips through block-with-override to encryption and Endpoint controls that restrict copying to USB, clipboard, and cloud upload. Two realistic policies anchor the lesson: blocking external sharing of credit-card data, and restricting labeled files from leaving managed devices on unmanaged USB. You will also use simulation mode, policy tips, alerts, and DLP analytics to roll out safely.
objectives: Describe Purview DLP and the workloads it protects, including Endpoint DLP on managed devices
Build DLP conditions from Sensitive Information Types and sensitivity labels with instance counts and confidence
Select appropriate actions: policy tip, block, block with override, encrypt, and Endpoint restrictions
Configure Endpoint DLP to restrict copy to USB, clipboard, and cloud upload, plus print and network share
Roll out a policy safely using simulation/test mode, policy tips, and user education before enforcement
Author two realistic policies: block external credit-card sharing and restrict labeled files to unmanaged USB

quiz.q: What is the relationship between data classification and DLP?
options: DLP replaces classification entirely
Classification identifies what the data is; DLP enforces what users may do with that identified data
DLP only works on unclassified data
Classification is only needed for email, DLP only for endpoints
quiz.why: DLP conditions are written against the things classification produces: Sensitive Information Types and sensitivity labels. Classification answers 'what is this data,' and DLP answers 'what is allowed to happen to it.' Without classification, a DLP policy has nothing reliable to match on.

quiz.q: Which set of locations does a single Purview DLP policy potentially cover?
options: Only Exchange email
Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams chat and channel messages, and Endpoint (managed devices)
Only on-premises file servers
Only third-party SaaS apps
quiz.why: Purview DLP spans Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams messages, and Endpoint DLP on Windows and macOS managed devices (plus options like on-premises repositories and Defender for Cloud Apps). A single policy can select multiple of these locations, giving consistent enforcement across the data estate.

quiz.q: A policy uses 'Block with override.' What does this achieve compared to a plain block?
options: It silently allows the action with no record
It blocks the action but lets the user proceed after providing a business justification, which is logged
It always encrypts instead of blocking
It disables the policy for that user permanently
quiz.why: Block with override stops the risky action by default but allows the user to override, typically requiring a business justification or false-positive report, which is recorded. This balances protection with productivity and surfaces edge cases for tuning while keeping an audit trail.

quiz.q: Endpoint DLP is configured to restrict 'copy to removable USB' for files carrying the Highly Confidential label. Which prerequisite makes this enforceable?
options: The device must be unmanaged and personal
The device must be onboarded to Purview/Defender endpoint management so Endpoint DLP can monitor egress actions
The user must be a global administrator
The file must be stored only in Exchange
quiz.why: Endpoint DLP only works on devices onboarded to Microsoft Purview / Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Once onboarded, the endpoint agent can observe and restrict egress activities such as copying to USB, clipboard, cloud upload, printing, and network shares for labeled or SIT-matched files.

quiz.q: Why should you run a new DLP policy in simulation (test) mode before enforcement?
options: Simulation mode encrypts all matching files immediately
It shows what the policy would match and which actions would fire, so you can gauge impact and false positives without disrupting users
It is required to license DLP
Simulation mode only works for Teams
quiz.why: Simulation (test) mode evaluates the policy and reports matches and would-be actions, optionally showing policy tips, without actually blocking anything. This lets you measure false positives, estimate user impact, and tune conditions before turning on enforcement, avoiding a disruptive big-bang rollout.

quiz.q: Design a DLP policy, in two to four sentences, that blocks external sharing of credit-card data while remaining usable for staff who occasionally have a legitimate need. Name the location, condition, action, and rollout approach.
quiz.answer: Create a DLP policy scoped to Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams with a condition that content contains the built-in Credit Card Number SIT at high confidence with a low instance threshold, and that the content is shared with people outside the organization. Use a 'Block with override' action so external sharing is stopped by default but a user with a genuine need can proceed with a logged business justification, and show a policy tip explaining the rule. Roll it out first in simulation mode with policy tips on to measure false positives, then enable enforcement once the match rate looks clean and generate alerts for any overrides. This protects regulated data while keeping a controlled escape hatch and an audit trail for legitimate cases.
quiz.why: A strong answer ties together the correct location set, a label/SIT-based condition with a recipient-is-external check, a block-with-override action for the legitimate-need requirement, and a simulation-first rollout, which is exactly the safe, real-world DLP pattern.

body_markdown:
## From Knowing to Controlling

In the previous lesson you taught Purview to **identify** sensitive data with SITs, trainable classifiers, and labels. **Data Loss Prevention (DLP)** is the control that decides **what users are allowed to do** with that identified data. A DLP policy watches for sensitive content in motion, an email to an outside recipient, a file shared with an external guest, a document copied to a USB stick, and applies actions ranging from a gentle tip to a hard block. The two halves fit together: classification provides the *what*, DLP provides the *what's allowed*.

## Where DLP Applies: Locations

A single Purview DLP policy can protect multiple **locations**:

- **Exchange Online** - outbound and internal email.
- **SharePoint** and **OneDrive** - files at rest and when shared.
- **Teams** - chat and channel messages.
- **Endpoint (Devices)** - managed Windows and macOS devices via **Endpoint DLP**, controlling local egress like USB, clipboard, and cloud upload.
- Plus **on-premises repositories** and **Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps** for broader SaaS coverage.

Choosing locations thoughtfully matters: an email-only policy will not stop a user dragging a file to a thumb drive. That gap is exactly what **Endpoint DLP** closes.

## Conditions: Built on Classification

A DLP rule's **conditions** describe what to match. The most common building blocks are:

- **Content contains** a **Sensitive Information Type** (e.g. *Credit Card Number*), with a **confidence level** and a **minimum instance count** (one card vs. fifty cards is very different risk).
- **Content contains** a **sensitivity label** (e.g. *Highly Confidential*) or a retention label.
- **Context** conditions: recipient is **external**, content is **shared with people outside the organization**, sender domain, attachment type, and more.

You combine conditions with AND/OR and group them. A typical rule reads: *content contains Credit Card Number (high confidence, 1+ instances) AND is shared with people outside my organization*.

## Actions: From Tips to Hard Blocks

Once a rule matches, **actions** decide the outcome. Common actions, roughly increasing in strictness:

- **Policy tip** - a non-blocking, educational message shown to the user in Outlook, Office, or Teams. Pure user education.
- **Notify** - email the user or admins; log an event.
- **Restrict access / encrypt** - apply rights protection or restrict who can access the shared content.
- **Block with override** - block by default but let the user proceed with a logged **business justification** or **false-positive report**.
- **Block** - hard stop, no override.

For Endpoint locations, additional **Endpoint actions** apply: **restrict copy to removable USB**, **restrict clipboard copy**, **restrict cloud / web upload**, **restrict print**, **restrict copy to network share**, and **restrict access by unallowed apps**, each settable to *Audit*, *Block with override*, or *Block*.

## Endpoint DLP in Depth

**Endpoint DLP** extends enforcement to the device itself, where users actually exfiltrate data. It only works on devices **onboarded** to Microsoft Purview / Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Once onboarded, the endpoint agent observes egress activities and enforces your actions:

- Copying a labeled file to an **unmanaged USB** drive.
- Pasting sensitive content into a browser or chat via the **clipboard**.
- Uploading to **unsanctioned cloud apps** or personal web services.
- **Printing** or copying to a **network share**.

You can also define **printer groups**, **removable storage device groups**, and **network share groups** so that, for example, corporate-approved encrypted USB drives are allowed while all others are blocked.

## Two Realistic Policies

**Policy A - Block external sharing of credit-card data.**

```text
Locations:   Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams
Condition:   Content contains SIT "Credit Card Number"
             (High confidence, 1+ instances)
             AND content is shared with people outside the org
Action:      Block with override (require business justification)
User:        Policy tip explaining the rule
Alerts:      High-severity alert on every override
```

**Policy B - Restrict labeled files from leaving managed devices on unmanaged USB.**

```text
Location:    Devices (Endpoint DLP, onboarded devices only)
Condition:   Content contains sensitivity label "Highly Confidential"
Endpoint actions:
             Copy to removable USB ......... Block
             (allow approved "Corporate USB" device group)
             Copy to clipboard ............. Block with override
             Upload to cloud / web ......... Block
             Print ......................... Audit
User:        Policy tip; override requires justification
```

Policy A keeps regulated card data inside the tenant with a controlled escape hatch. Policy B ensures your most sensitive labeled documents cannot trivially walk out on a personal thumb drive while still permitting approved hardware.

## Roll Out Safely, Then Monitor

Never flip a new DLP policy straight to enforce. Use this sequence:

1. **Simulation / test mode** - the policy evaluates and reports what it *would* match and which actions *would* fire, without disrupting anyone. Review the would-be matches to gauge false positives and impact.
2. **Test with policy tips** - turn tips on in test mode so users start seeing guidance and you collect feedback.
3. **Enforce** - once the match rate is clean, enable enforcement.

After go-live, run the operation from data: the **DLP Alerts dashboard** surfaces matches, overrides, and false-positive reports, and **DLP analytics / activity explorer** show trends so you can tune conditions, reduce noise, and prove control effectiveness to auditors. DLP is never 'set and forget'; it is a continuous loop of measure, tune, and educate.

slides.title: Classification Plus DLP
bullets: Classification answers: what is this data?
DLP answers: what is the user allowed to do with it?
DLP conditions are built from SITs and sensitivity labels
The two halves are designed to work together
slides.narration: DLP and classification are two halves of one system. Classification produces the things DLP matches on: sensitive information types and sensitivity labels. Classification tells you what the data is, and DLP enforces what is allowed to happen to it, whether that is a tip, a block, or an encryption action. Without good classification, DLP has nothing reliable to act on.

slides.title: Where DLP Applies: Locations
bullets: Exchange email, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams messages
Endpoint DLP on managed Windows and macOS devices
Optionally on-premises and Defender for Cloud Apps
One policy can span several locations for consistency
slides.narration: A single DLP policy can cover many locations: Exchange email, SharePoint and OneDrive files, Teams chat, and the endpoint itself. An email-only policy will never stop a user dragging a file onto a USB drive, which is exactly the gap Endpoint DLP closes. Choosing the right combination of locations is the first design decision in any policy.

slides.title: Conditions Built on Classification
bullets: Content contains a SIT, with confidence and instance count
Content contains a sensitivity or retention label
Context: recipient external, shared outside org, file type
Combine with AND/OR and grouping
slides.narration: Conditions describe what to match. The workhorses are content contains a sensitive information type, tuned by confidence and a minimum instance count, and content contains a sensitivity label. You layer in context like recipient is external or shared with people outside the organization. A classic rule is: contains a credit card number at high confidence and is shared externally.

slides.title: Actions: Tips to Hard Blocks
bullets: Policy tip: non-blocking user education
Restrict access or encrypt the content
Block with override: proceed with logged justification
Block: hard stop, no override
slides.narration: When a rule matches, actions decide the outcome, from least to most strict. A policy tip just educates. Restrict or encrypt limits access. Block with override stops the action by default but lets a user proceed with a logged business justification, which is the productivity-friendly middle ground. And a plain block is a hard stop. Most mature policies favour block with override to keep an audit trail.

slides.title: Endpoint DLP Controls
bullets: Works only on devices onboarded to Purview/Defender
Restrict copy to USB, clipboard, and cloud/web upload
Also print and copy to network share
Define approved USB, printer, and network-share groups
slides.narration: Endpoint DLP enforces at the device, where exfiltration actually happens. The device must be onboarded to Purview and Defender for Endpoint. Then the agent can restrict copying to USB, clipboard pasting, cloud and web uploads, printing, and network-share copies. You can whitelist approved hardware, for example allowing a corporate encrypted USB device group while blocking all others.

slides.title: Policy A: Block External Card Data
bullets: Locations: Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams
Condition: Credit Card Number SIT + shared externally
Action: Block with override and business justification
High-severity alert on every override
slides.code:
Condition: SIT "Credit Card Number" (High, 1+)
           AND shared with people outside org
Action:    Block with override (justification)
Alert:     High severity on override
slides.narration: Here is our first realistic policy. Across email, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams, we match credit card numbers at high confidence that are shared externally, and we block with override so a genuine business need can proceed with a logged justification. Every override raises a high-severity alert. This protects regulated data while leaving a controlled, audited escape hatch.

slides.title: Policy B: Restrict Labeled Files on USB
bullets: Location: Devices (Endpoint DLP only)
Condition: file carries Highly Confidential label
Block copy to unmanaged USB; allow approved device group
Block cloud upload; clipboard block-with-override; print audit
slides.code:
Label:  Highly Confidential
USB:    Block (allow "Corporate USB" group)
Cloud:  Block upload
Clip:   Block with override
Print:  Audit
slides.narration: Our second policy lives entirely on the endpoint. Any file carrying the Highly Confidential label cannot be copied to an unmanaged USB drive, though an approved corporate USB device group is still allowed. Cloud upload is blocked, clipboard is block with override, and printing is audited so we keep visibility. This stops your crown-jewel documents from walking out on a personal thumb drive.

slides.title: Roll Out Safely, Then Monitor
bullets: Start in simulation/test mode: see matches without blocking
Add policy tips in test mode to educate and gather feedback
Enforce only once false positives are low
Monitor via DLP Alerts dashboard and activity explorer
slides.narration: Never flip a new policy straight to enforce. Run it in simulation mode to see what it would match and how many false positives you would generate. Turn on policy tips in test mode to start educating users, then enforce once the signal is clean. After go-live, watch the DLP Alerts dashboard and activity explorer, and keep tuning. DLP is a continuous loop of measure, tune, and educate, never set and forget.
